questions.q: Why should you build file paths with path.join instead of adding strings with +?
questions.explain: path.join follows the path rules of the system the program runs on: one separator between parts, .. handled, \ on Windows. It does not touch the disk, and it keeps a relative path relative (that is path.resolve's job).
options: It uses exactly one separator, understands .., and uses the right separator for the system
It checks that the file really exists on the disk
It is faster, because + copies the strings twice
It turns the path into an absolute path that starts at the root

questions.q: What does this print on macOS or Linux?
questions.explain: path.join removes the extra separator. Adding the strings keeps both slashes, which is exactly the bug the lesson warns about.

questions.q: What does this print on macOS or Linux?
questions.explain: .. means "the folder above", and path.join applies it. Each .. cancels the part before it, so a/b/../../c is just c.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: extname only gives the last extension, with its dot. basename is the whole file name, and dirname is the folder it is in, without a slash at the end.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A file name without a dot has no extension, so extname returns an empty string (not undefined). When there is one, the dot is included.

questions.q: What does path.resolve("tasks.json") return?
questions.explain: path.resolve builds an absolute path from the current working directory, the folder the program was started from. That is not always the folder your script is in.
options: An absolute path: the current working directory followed by tasks.json
The path of the file next to the script that is running

questions.q: Your script needs data/tasks.json, which sits next to the script. It must work whatever folder the program is started from. Which path should you use?
questions.explain: import.meta.dirname is the folder of the current file. The other three all start from the working directory, so they break when you run the program from another folder.

questions.q: A user asks for a file called /etc/passwd. What does this print on Linux?
questions.explain: .. climbs out of the folder, and an absolute name like /etc/passwd ignores the folder completely. That is why you must check the resolved path, not the name the user typed.

questions.q: An API serves files with path.join("uploads", name), where name comes from the URL. What is the danger?
questions.explain: This attack is called path traversal. path.join happily follows .., so it can reach any file the server can read, such as keys and passwords.
options: A name like ../.env walks out of the uploads folder and can leak secret files (path traversal)
A long name makes the server run out of memory
The name may contain spaces, which path.join cannot handle
There is no danger, because path.join only works inside the current folder

questions.q: You have const full = path.resolve(uploads, name), where uploads is an absolute path. Which check correctly refuses files outside the uploads folder?
questions.explain: Check the resolved path, and include the separator. Without path.sep, a neighbour folder such as uploads-old passes. Checking only the name misses /etc/passwd and a/../../x.

questions.q: What does this print on Linux?
questions.explain: "/srv/uploads-old/..." does start with the text "/srv/uploads", so the short check lets it through. Adding path.sep (/) makes the check mean "inside the folder".

questions.q: What does this print? (It works in a new temporary folder.)
questions.explain: writeFile replaces everything in the file, so the second writeFile throws away the first two lines. appendFile adds to the end.
options:
Buy milk
Call Ada
Write report
Pay rent

Buy milk
Call Ada
Pay rent

questions.q: You want to add one line to the end of a log file and keep what is already there. Which function do you use?
questions.explain: appendFile adds to the end (and creates the file if it is missing). writeFile starts the file over, which would delete the old log lines.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With "utf8" you get text. Without it, readFile gives you the raw bytes as a Buffer.

questions.q: What does { recursive: true } do in await mkdir("data/2026/logs", { recursive: true })?
questions.explain: With recursive, mkdir makes data, data/2026 and data/2026/logs as needed, and is fine when they are already there. That makes it safe to call every time before writing.
options: It also creates the missing parent folders, and does not fail if the folder already exists
It creates the folder and copies every file from the current folder into it
It deletes the folder first, then creates it empty
It creates the folder in every subfolder of the current folder

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: recursive accepts an existing folder. Without it, mkdir throws an error whose code is EEXIST: "already exists".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: readdir lists folders as well as files. stat gives the size in bytes: "Buy milk\n" is 9 bytes, because the line break counts too.

questions.q: Why should a server not call readFileSync while it handles a request?
questions.explain: Sync functions stop the whole program while they wait. That is fine once at start-up, but in a request handler it freezes all other requests. Use node:fs/promises and await.
options: It blocks the event loop until the disk answers, so every other user has to wait
It cannot read files bigger than 1 KB
It always returns a Buffer, never text
It only works in the browser

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing file throws. The error's code is ENOENT ("error: no entry"), and the message names the file. Your code should check error.code, not the message text.
options:
ENOENT
ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'no-such-file-7c1e.txt'

EEXIST
ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'no-such-file-7c1e.txt'

questions.q: Which catch block is right for reading a settings file that may not exist yet?
questions.explain: Handle only the error you expect, and throw the rest again. Returning defaults for every error hides real problems like broken JSON or EACCES (no permission).
options: if (error.message.includes("no such")) return defaults; and nothing else

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call finds no file, so it returns the defaults. The second file exists but holds broken JSON: that is not ENOENT, so the SyntaxError is thrown again instead of being hidden.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: You tried to read a folder as if it were a file. The code EISDIR means "this is a directory".

questions.q: A server wants to start one worker per processor core. Where does it find the number of cores?
questions.explain: node:os describes the machine: platform, processor, memory and line ending. availableParallelism() says how many things the processor can run at once.

questions.q: What does os.platform() return on a Mac?
questions.explain: macOS is built on a system called Darwin, so Node.js says "darwin". Windows is "win32" (even on 64-bit), and Linux is "linux".

questions.q: You need a token for a password-reset link. Which is safe?
questions.explain: Tokens must be unguessable. Math.random() can be predicted, a time can be guessed, and a hash of the e-mail is the same every time for anyone who knows the e-mail. node:crypto uses the system's secure random source.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A UUID is 36 characters (32 hex digits and 4 dashes). Each byte becomes 2 hex characters, so 16 bytes give 32. Every call gives a new random value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same input always gives the same hash, and a small change gives a different one. The length is fixed: SHA-256 in hex is always 64 characters, however long the input is.

questions.q: Which sentence about a hash like SHA-256 is true?
questions.explain: A hash is one-way: same input, same fingerprint, but no way back. That makes it good for checking whether a file has changed. Encryption is different, because it can be undone with a key.
options: It is a fixed-length fingerprint of the data, and you cannot turn it back into the data
It is a way to encrypt data so you can decrypt it later with a key
It gives a different result every time, like randomUUID()
Its length grows with the size of the input

questions.q: Why should you not store passwords as SHA-256 hashes?
questions.explain: Speed is good for file fingerprints and bad for passwords. A password hash must be slow and salted so guessing is expensive. You will use one in the ZudoJS authentication lesson.
options: SHA-256 is fast, so an attacker with your database can try billions of guesses per second; passwords need a slow, salted hash
SHA-256 can be turned back into the password with the right key
SHA-256 hashes are too long to store in a database
SHA-256 gives a different hash each time, so the login check would fail

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every listener for the event runs, in the order it was added, and they run synchronously during emit. So both lines appear before after.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A once listener is removed after its first call. The on listener stays, so it runs for both tasks.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The "error" event is special: with no listener, emit throws it. Once a listener exists, the listener receives the error instead.
options:
thrown: disk full
handled: disk full

thrown: disk full
thrown: disk full

questions.q: What happens to a Node.js program when a stream emits "error" and nothing listens for it (and nothing catches it)?
questions.explain: An unheard "error" event is thrown. Always add an "error" listener to emitters that can fail, such as servers and streams.
options: emit throws, the error is uncaught, and the program ends
The error is ignored and the stream carries on
Node.js prints a warning and retries the operation
The error is saved and given to the next listener that is added

questions.q: The task store emits "added" instead of calling the logger and the mailer itself. What is the main benefit?
questions.explain: Events keep code apart. Note that listeners are not run in the background: they run synchronously during emit.
options: The code that adds tasks does not need to know who reacts; you can add or remove reactions without changing it
Events make the code run faster than normal function calls
Listeners run in the background, so adding a task never waits for them
Events save the tasks to the disk automatically

questions.q: The task store's save writes to a temporary file and then renames it over tasks.json. Why?
questions.explain: If the program crashes halfway through writing, only the temporary file is broken; the old tasks.json is still whole. It does not fix two saves at once: that race still loses a task.
options: A rename happens all at once, so a crash while writing never leaves a half-written tasks.json
Renaming a file is the only way to change its contents in Node.js
It makes a backup copy of every old version of the file
It stops two saves at the same moment from losing a task

questions.q: Why does the temporary file name in save contain randomUUID()?
questions.explain: If two saves used the same temporary name, they could mix their writes into one file. A unique name per save keeps them apart.
options: So two saves never write into the same temporary file
So nobody can guess the name and read the tasks
So the file is deleted automatically after one hour
Because rename only accepts names that contain a UUID

questions.q: This copies how the JSON-file store adds a task: read, wait, then write. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both calls read the list while it is still empty, so both pick id 1, and the second write replaces the first. One task is lost with no error. This is a race condition.

questions.q: Your API saves tasks in a JSON file, and two users sometimes add tasks at the same moment. What does the lesson say is the real fix?
questions.explain: A JSON file works for one person at a time. Two writers read the same old list, and the last write wins. Databases exist to solve exactly this.
options: Use a database, which is built to handle many writes at once
Write to a temporary file and rename it
Add a listener for the "error" event

questions.q: The task program is started as node tasks.js add "Buy milk". This line copies how it reads the command. What does it print?
questions.explain: process.argv starts with the path of node and of the script, so slice(2) skips them. The quotes in the shell keep Buy milk together as one value.

questions.q: The store picks the next id with Math.max(0, ...ids) + 1. What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.max() with no numbers gives -Infinity, so the store adds 0 as a starting value. Then an empty list gives id 1, and the next id is always one more than the biggest.

questions.q: Finish isInside(folder, full). Both are absolute paths with / as the separator. Return true only when full is a file inside folder. A neighbour folder like /srv/uploads-old must not pass, and neither must the folder itself.
questions.explain: Add the separator before comparing: full.startsWith(folder + "/"). That is the same idea as uploads + path.sep in the lesson.

questions.q: Finish countByExtension(names). It returns an object counting the files per extension. The extension is the text from the last dot, including the dot, like path.extname. A name without a dot counts as "(none)". The program should print {"(none)":1,".md":1,".pdf":1,".txt":2}.
questions.explain: Find the last dot with lastIndexOf(".") and slice from there; no dot (-1) means "(none)". Count with counts[ext] = (counts[ext] ?? 0) + 1.

questions.q: Finish loadOrDefault(read, fallback). It calls read() and returns its result. If read() throws an error whose code is "ENOENT", return fallback. Any other error must be thrown again.
questions.explain: Wrap the call in try/catch, return the fallback only when error.code === "ENOENT", and throw error for everything else, so real problems are not hidden.
questions.expected:
saved tasks
no tasks
re-thrown: EACCES

questions.explain: Keep a Map from event name to an array of listeners. emit loops over the array for that name; ?? [] handles names nobody listens for.

log: Buy milk

removed: Buy milk

questions.q: Finish complete(tasks, id). It marks the task with that id as done and returns it. When no task has that id, it throws an Error with the message task 7 not found (using the real id).
questions.explain: Use find to get the task. If it is undefined, throw an error with a clear message; otherwise set done and return it.
questions.expected:
Write report true
task 7 not found

questions.q: randomBytes(n).toString("hex") writes each byte as two hexadecimal characters. Finish toHex(bytes), which does the same for an array of numbers from 0 to 255. The program should print 00ff10a7.
questions.explain: b.toString(16) writes a number in hexadecimal. Small numbers need a leading zero, so pad each to 2 characters with padStart(2, "0"), then join them.
